H&P – Detailed

Consult Summary:
27-year-old woman with known asthma presents with 2–3 day history of worsening wheeze, cough, and exertional shortness of breath not relieved by salbutamol; advised to increase inhaled steroid dose and arrange urgent face-to-face GP review.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Tight chest, wheeze, cough, and shortness of breath.  
• Onset & course: Began 2–3 days ago while running; persists with brisk walking; no improvement after usual salbutamol use.  
• Severity/progression: Now using salbutamol every morning/evening and as needed; symptoms ongoing.  
• Associated symptoms: Wheeze, dry cough; denies sputum production.  
• Exacerbating factors: Physical exertion (running, brisk walking).  
• Relieving factors: None—blue inhaler ineffective.  
• Review of systems: No fever, no hospital admissions, no recent infections mentioned.  
• Previous asthma history: Last asthma attack 3–4 years ago; never required oral steroids or hospital admission; last asthma review ~2 years ago. Baseline peak-flow ~380 L/min (self-reported); no current reading available.

Past Medical History:
• Asthma – long-standing; generally well-controlled until current episode. No prior oral steroid courses; no hospitalizations.  
• Possible eczema (patient uncertain; uses topical emollient/steroid).  
• Allergic rhinitis/hay fever.

Medications:
• Salbutamol inhaler (blue) – dose/route/frequency not documented; patient using prn and morning/evening prophylactically.  
• Clenil (beclomethasone) inhaler – previously 3 puffs BID; advised to increase to 4 puffs BID.  
• Cetraben cream – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Hydrocortisone cream – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Bactroban (mupirocin) cream – dose/route/frequency not documented.  

Allergies:
• No known drug allergies.  
• Hay fever (environmental).

Social History:
• No information on smoking, alcohol, or drug use documented.  
• Lives at home; no other social details provided.

Family History:
• Brother with asthma.  
• Sister with eczema.

Physical Examination:
(Not performed during virtual consult; no vitals provided.)

Investigations:
• Patient-reported usual peak flow: ~380 L/min.  
• No current objective measurements or tests available.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1: Suspected mild asthma exacerbation
  • Assessment: 2–3 days of increased SOB, wheeze, cough; inadequate relief with salbutamol; no red-flag features but deteriorating control.  
  • Plan:  
    – Increase Clenil to 4 puffs twice daily (higher inhaled steroid dose).  
    – Continue salbutamol inhaler up to every 2 hours as needed; advise that frequent use indicates poor control.  
    – Book urgent face-to-face GP appointment within next few days for chest examination, peak-flow measurement, and formal asthma review.  
    – Possible need for oral steroids and/or antibiotics after assessment.  
    – Safety-net: Attend A&E immediately if breathing worsens or if requiring salbutamol very frequently despite increased Clenil.

Issue 2: Long-term asthma management
  • Plan:  
    – Arrange formal annual asthma review (spirometry, action plan, inhaler technique).  
    – Provide/renew peak-flow meter for home monitoring.  
    – Reinforce trigger avoidance and correct inhaler technique.

Issue 3: Possible eczema / skin care
  • Plan:  
    – Continue topical emollient (Cetraben) and hydrocortisone cream as required.  
    – Mention during upcoming GP visit if skin symptoms persist or worsen.

General Plan items:
• No medication allergies documented; confirm at next visit.  
• Update electronic medical record with current inhaler regimen and action plan.

Quality checks:

● Missing but expected elements: smoking status, alcohol intake, occupation, vitals, current peak-flow reading, full medication doses/routes/frequencies, complete allergy list.  
● Internal conflicts: None significant (initial “fever” clarified as “hay fever”).  
● Transcript quality: Minor inaudible sections and medication name uncertainty; core clinical information intact.
